item.title: Reliability of Fisher-information bounds for dielectric metalenses: a site-resolved RCWA audit
item.description: arXiv:2611.07077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We assess the reliability of localization precision predicted for a 1716-nanopillar dielectric metalens using a site-resolved complex RCWA library and a vectorial Poisson Fisher model. An independent calculation reproduces the archived local axial Cramer-Rao bound of 20.7738 nm to within 0.0044 nm, yielding 20.7695 nm under the same ideal detector and 3000 detected signal photons. High-order periodic-cell calculations reveal a 0.1335 rad phase difference at a selected diameter; different substrate-index assumptions prevent attributing this difference solely to modal truncation. Replacing the recalculated coefficients at 39 actual sites changes the bound to 20.7522 nm. Restricted phase-mask benchmarks and pixel-integration checks further distinguish a stable statistical prediction from electromagnetic convergence. We provide a reproducible, model-conditional benchmark, not a physical-device performance claim.
item.dc:creator: J. Sumaya-Martinez, O. Olmos-Lopez

item.title: Dispersive Corrections to Electromagnetic Energy and Power Flux Are Imprints of Eliminated Degrees of Freedom
item.description: arXiv:2611.07243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a spatially dispersive medium the electromagnetic energy and flux are given by the frequency and wave-vector derivatives of the constitutive parameters, a result known as the Agranovich--Ginzburg (AG) formulas. Here, we clarify the physical meaning of the derivative terms in these relations and show that they measure the energy and flux carried by the degrees of freedom of the internal field-matter dynamics that the Maxwellian constitutive description hides. We construct an extended state-space model of such dynamics for a wide class of temporally and spatially dispersive media, from which the Maxwellian constitutive relations follow upon elimination of the internal variables, the effective material operator resulting from the Schur complement of the eliminated internal block. A congruence identity relates this complement to the extended state-space description, which allows us to extend the AG formulas to general bianisotropic media and to establish the conditions of their validity in the presence of dissipation. The AG dispersive corrections are thus the imprints of the eliminated degrees of freedom rather than independent constitutive postulates. They hold for fields driven at arbitrary real frequency and wave vector, and not only for eigenmodes, provided that the sources act on the fields alone and that any dissipation is carried by the electromagnetic subsystem. We verify the construction on the Lorentz, Drude, magnetized-plasma, and hydrodynamic models, the last of which describes a nonlocal metal. Additionally, a capacitively loaded wire medium is treated in the Supplemental Material.
item.dc:creator: Stanislav Maslovski, Constantin Simovski

item.title: A nonlinear interface for phase transduction
item.description: arXiv:2611.07316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Broadband nonlinear frequency conversion mixes multiple input frequencies, complicating the transfer of programmed spectral phase between widely separated spectral bands. Here we identify and experimentally realize a quasi-linear phase-transduction regime enabled by broad phase-matching acceptance and effective localization of the complex frequency-mixing response. This selectivity can arise from coherent interference without narrowing the pump spectrum. We implement this regime through dispersive four-wave mixing in an argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber, transferring spectral phase from 1032-nm near-infrared signals to 344-nm ultraviolet idlers. Transient-grating frequency-resolved optical gating reveals frequency-inverted, phase-conjugating transfer of quadratic dispersion, localized phase steps, and low-frequency sinusoidal modulation. After correction for the modeled pump-induced phase background, the quadratic and step responses exhibit approximately linear point-by-point correlations. With increasing pump chirp, the transferred phase steps become more sharply preserved, and the fitted phase-transfer gains approach unity, consistent with enhanced effective localization. These results demonstrate quasi-linear spectral-phase transduction in a co-propagating broadband nonlinear interaction without spatially separating its spectral components.
item.dc:creator: Linshan Sun, Hao Zhang, Cameron Leary, Alex Amador, Sergio Carbajo

item.title: Stable dissipative topological solitons in media with even-order dispersion
item.description: arXiv:2611.07467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The formation and dynamics of dissipative solitons are governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity, alongside the gain-loss balance. While it is known that dispersion orders beyond the conventional second order support stable solitons, the possibility of the creation of dissipative topological solitons in this setting was not explored. Here, we reveal a class of stable dissipative solitons enabled by the pure-high-even-order dispersion (PHEOD), with dispersion orders m=4, 6, 8, and 10. The resulting dissipative topological solitons (DTSs) and moving topological solitons (MTSs) are dark-type structures featuring a zero-amplitude point that separates two CW backgrounds with opposite signs. In particular, the PHEOD solitons feature oscillatory tails, which are not present in the conventional dark states. The linear-stability analysis confirms full robustness of the PHEOD-supported DTSs and MTSs. We also explore collision dynamics of MTSs, whose repulsive interactions are inelastic, leading either to rebound, accompanied by emission of dispersive radiation, or complete fusion. These findings establish PHEOD as a means for the generation of new species of dissipative solitons, and broaden the variety of nonlinear modes available to experimental studies in nonlinear optics.
item.dc:creator: Xianan Sun, Dongdong Wang, Dumitru Mihalache, David Laroze, Boris A. Malomed, Pengfei Li

item.title: Experimental demonstration of dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal emission at moderate magnetic fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.07564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which requires emissivity and absorptivity to be equal at each wavelength, angle, and polarization. This in turn places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies as well as heat transfer. This constraint can however be overcome using magneto-optic semiconductors, which break Lorentz reciprocity under an applied magnetic field. However, in most prior experimental demonstrations, nonreciprocity has been restricted to TM polarization, since the electric field of TE-polarized light is parallel to the applied magnetic field. Here, we experimentally demonstrate nonreciprocal absorption in both polarizations at the same wavelengths and angles from a single structure, wherein a germanium Mie-resonant metasurface on a doped InAs layer scatters TE-polarized light into near fields with components perpendicular to the magnetic field, allowing the magneto-optic response of the InAs to act on them. Under a 0.48 T field from a permanent Halbach array, this structure exhibits a difference in absorptivity between $+B$ and $-B$ of 0.035 in both TE and TM polarization at 16.6 $\mu$m. Our approach shows that the magneto-optic response of a planar semiconductor and the resonances of a dielectric metasurface can be designed together, offering a potential route to dual-polarization nonreciprocity at fields available from permanent magnets for emerging energy and heat transfer technologies.
item.dc:creator: Mason Christiansen, Jae S. Hwang, Yi Jie Lin, Aryan Zaveri, Tianjun Li, Daniel Cui, Baolai Liang, Aaswath P. Raman

item.title: Simulation of Refraction Through Voxel Volumes
item.description: arXiv:2611.07690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ray tracing in X-ray science has typically been limited to descriptions where refraction occurs only at interfaces, ignoring the refraction occurring due to the continuous variations in index of refraction in the bulk of a material, as are common in biological samples like bone. We propose a method to simulate X-ray images directly on voxel grids using curved rays. We first validate this method compared to a model with an analytical solution, and then investigate the effects of voxel size, interpolation choice, and illumination to grid alignment on a few simulated test objects. From these investigations, we make several recommendations to guide simulations using these techniques.
item.dc:creator: Rainier Mobley, Jean Michel L\'etang, Max Langer

item.title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers
item.description: arXiv:2611.07729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short mode-evolution couplers have been designed with several seemingly different approaches, including fast quasi-adiabatic dynamics (FAQUAD), counter-diabatic (CD) driving realized by tailoring waveguide widths and spacing, CD driving realized by axis bending, and numerical optimization of the coupler geometry. Using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers--Henneberger frame of the bent coupler, we show that these approaches belong to the same design space. The three geometric parameters, width difference, spacing, and axis tilt, act on the light through two functions only: the coupling strength, set by the spacing, and an effective detuning, set by the width difference and the axis curvature. The gauge, bent, and mixed realizations of a CD coupler are therefore the same device and have the same bandwidth. The bandwidth is set by the angle $\chi$ between the light and the field that steers it on the Bloch sphere, integrated along the device as $\int\sin^2\chi dz$, and for a CD coupler this integral is set by the reference alone. This leads to a lithography-aware design rule: make the reference as adiabatic as the minimum gap allows, by narrowing its spacing at the anticrossing, and let exact CD suppress the remaining nonadiabatic coupling. In beam propagation method (BPM) simulations on a polymer platform, a 500\um{} coupler designed this way, without numerical optimization, maintains ${>}99\%$ transfer over 274~nm at a minimum edge gap of 1.05\um, compared with 150~nm for the CD coupler of a fixed-spacing reference at nearly the same gap. Particle swarm optimization of the geometry with BPM in the loop does not exceed the design rule. Three-dimensional BPM of the BCB channel waveguides also confirms these conclusions.
item.dc:creator: S. -Y. Tseng

item.title: Laser fabrication of vibrating microcavities on silicon: Formation dynamics and frequency tunability
item.description: arXiv:2611.07742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laser processing of silicon has long since become a standard method for wafer dicing, surface texturing, re-crystallization after ion implantation, as well as surface amorphization, to name a few examples. Here, we introduce a novel concept, the fabrication of vibrating microcavities in a commercial platform, Si wafers covered by a thick SiO2 layer, acting as a membrane. We demonstrate that by exposing our material system to single ultrashort laser pulses above the evaporation threshold of Si, a controlled delamination of the cover layer without fracture can be achieved, leading to the formation of a microcavity accompanied by a surface bulging up to 1.5 micrometer. The formation dynamics of the microcavities has been investigated by time-resolved optical probe techniques. Ultrafast pump-probe microscopy resolves the initial stages of substrate melting, the onset of layer expansion followed by relaxation. Real-time reflectivity measurements with nanosecond resolution resolve the long lived, highly complex oscillation process of the membrane, extending over tens of microseconds. The formed cavities can be re-excited at low fluence without damage or degradation, featuring vibrations at single frequencies with high Q factors. The frequencies can be tuned continuously from 8 MHz up to 19 MHz by adjusting the fabrication fluence. A simple classical model is found to well describe the behavior of the membranes. Our results pave the way for applications in micro- and nanooptics and acoustics, in great part due to the commercial availability of the Si-SiO2 platform and the simplicity of the fabrication method. An extension to the field of microelectromechanical system (MEMS) of this technology is proposed.
item.dc:creator: Belen Valiente, Gonzalo Gomez-Munoz, Mario Garcia-Lechuga, Irene Solana, Fernando Agull\'o-Rueda, David Grojo, Angel Rodriguez-Fernandez, Javier Solis, Jan Siegel

item.title: Continuum Photonic Axion Insulators
item.description: arXiv:2611.07893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Here, I study the conditions for realizing an axion topology in a homogeneous inversion-symmetric electromagnetic continuum, in the absence of a crystalline lattice. I introduce a continuum inversion invariant expressed solely in terms of the spectral properties of the material response in the zero- and infinite-wave-vector limits. Surprisingly, it is found that standard gyrotropic-type material responses are strongly constrained and, under fairly general conditions, cannot open an axion gap within first-order perturbation theory. Based on an analogy between the effective response of crystalline photonic axion insulators and the optical response of centrosymmetric altermagnets, a class of spatially dispersive odd magnetoelectric couplings that can open an axion gap is identified. These findings suggest an interesting hierarchy of nonreciprocal mechanisms in electromagnetic continua: while uniform gyrotropy relates to Chern phases, odd magnetoelectric coupling relates to axion phases.
item.dc:creator: Mario G. Silveirinha

item.title: A Passive Intelligent Metasurface: A Network Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.07894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent metasurfaces enable advanced wave manipulation, including negative refraction, focusing, beam splitting and beam steering, with significant potential for practical applications. However, conventional approaches often rely on active metamaterials with gain, or demand computationally intensive solutions of inverse problems to find the optimal configuration. In this work, we use the scattering framework of quantum graph theory to derive an exact, analytic expression for configuration of a passive metasurface that produces a prescribed reflected wave field. The metasurface terminates a periodic lattice of waveguides and consists of an array of channels, each a tube of length $\ell_m$ ending in a vertex whose scattering parameter $\lambda_m$ sets how much of the wave is lost to the wall. For any prescribed incident and reflected field, the exact lengths and scattering parameters follow channel by channel, in closed form, from the ratio of the wave amplitudes returning to and leaving the lattice, and the metasurface is passive whenever this ratio does not exceed unity in modulus. We demonstrate the construction for both a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional metasurface. The one-dimensional metasurface terminates a two-dimensional lattice and steers, splits or perfectly absorbs Gaussian beams. The two-dimensional metasurface terminates a three-dimensional lattice and generates a prescribed image in a plane inside the lattice. In each case, we obtain the exact boundary properties that produce the effect.
item.dc:creator: Tristan Lawrie, Gregor Tanner, Luke Bennetts

item.title: Hybrid integration of a SESAM with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit
item.description: arXiv:2611.08057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The realization of high-performance femtosecond lasers on photonic integrated circuits (PICs) requires robust, low-loss coupling between a saturable absorber and a photonic waveguide. In this work, we demonstrate the hybrid integration of a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) with a silicon nitride (SiN) PIC by micro-assembly. This micro-assembly strategy transfers the non-linear functionality of the absorber onto the PIC. We characterize the linear and non-linear performance of an unbonded SESAM and of a SESAM bonded to inverse-tapered SiN waveguides. At 1560~nm, the bonded device shows a waveguide-coupled modulation depth of 5.2\%, a maximum reflectivity of 37.2\%, and a saturation fluence of 47~\textmu J/cm$^2$. This work demonstrates that SESAMs can be integrated directly onto silicon nitride-based PIC platforms and provides a pathway towards fully integrated, self-starting, chip-scale ultrafast lasers.
item.dc:creator: Amaryllis Verstraete, Tom Reep, Jan de Haan, Eero Koivusalo, Riku Isoaho, Thi Ngoc Lam Tran, Bart Kuyken, Kasper Van Gasse

item.title: Thermal Inverse Design: Tailoring the Transient Response of Resistive Micro-Heaters
item.description: arXiv:2611.08098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microheaters underpin a broad range of applications that require localized and dynamic thermal control. Engineering their spatial and temporal temperature distributions is therefore essential, yet conventional heater design relies largely on iterative trial and error involving numerous full-scale thermal simulations. Here, we introduce an inverse design algorithm for pulsed heating, a common operating modality in thermal processing, sensing, switching, and material characterization. The approach uses a single lithographic step to pattern the doped regions of a silicon microheater and, in principle, enables on-demand peak temperature distributions under transient voltage excitation within one closed design loop. The algorithm also incorporates practical fabrication constraints, including finite lithographic resolution. We demonstrate its versatility through three representative designs. First, an optimized heater achieves more than a 20-fold reduction in temperature nonuniformity compared with a conventional uniformly doped heater. Second, inverse-designed doping effectively cancels the thermal gradient in a heater connected in series with a diode. Third, the method generates prescribed linear temperature gradients on demand. These results establish inverse-designed doping as a scalable and fabrication-compatible approach for tailoring transient temperature distributions in resistive microheaters.
item.dc:creator: Muzhang Huang, Junhe Zhang, Khoi Phuong Dao, Juejun Hu, Hyun Jung Kim

item.title: Photonic Exceptional Topological Bound States in the Continuum
item.description: arXiv:2611.08103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exceptional bound states in the continuum (EBICs) arise when bound states in the continuum (BICs) with distinct intrinsic losses coalesce at exceptional points (EPs), combining continuum-embedded wave confinement with a non-analytic spectral response. However, conventional EBICs rely on precisely controlled modal coupling and intrinsic loss, making them fragile and difficult to realize experimentally. Here, we introduce bulk-band topology to mitigate this fragility and experimentally realize a photonic exceptional topological BIC (ETBIC) in spoof surface plasmon polariton waveguides by merging two symmetry-protected topological BICs (TBICs) to coalesce at an EP, with the topological design supporting robust localization under symmetry-preserving perturbations. By engineering an intrinsic loss contrast and tuning the intermodal coupling, we directly resolve the coalescence of the complex eigenfrequencies, accompanied by measured near-field distributions consistent with the exceptional eigenstate. Furthermore, weak perturbations induce approximately square-root eigenfrequency splitting, yielding an enhanced spectral response compared with the approximately linear frequency shift of an isolated TBIC. These results establish bulk-band topology as a design principle for exceptional BIC engineering and provide a foundation for EBIC-based photonic sensing.
item.dc:creator: Liren Chen, Jingming Chen, Zhen Gao

item.title: Characterization and Suppression of Parasitic Back-Reflection Noise in Transponder-Type Heterodyne Interferometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.08110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transponder-type heterodyne interferometry is a versatile metrological technique for high-precision measurements, with applications in Earth's gravity-field recovery, space-based gravitational-wave detection, deep-space ranging, and Doppler tracking. However, parasitic back-reflections can contaminate phase readout and degrade measurement sensitivity. To characterize and suppress this noise, we constructed a transponder-type interferometer with coaxially aligned counter-propagating beams, achieving stable operation at a received optical power of 720 pW. An adjustable reflecting system was introduced into the master-side transmit path to simulate back-reflection under realistic conditions. Optical path scans and model fitting showed that phase errors vary periodically with the relative phase between the main and parasitic interference signals, which defines the working point. Assisted by {\pi} measurement, adjustment to low-sensitivity working points was combined with balanced detection to suppress back-reflection phase noise, achieving maximum suppression factors of 77 for single-frequency phase errors and 23 for band-limited phase-noise amplitude spectral density. {\pi} measurement also enabled working point diagnosis at 3.8 nW back-reflection power, confirming its applicability under weak back-reflection conditions. These results provide an effective approach for in situ back-reflection characterization and phase-noise suppression in transponder-type heterodyne interferometry.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyang Lin, Xin Xu, Xinhang Lyu, Peijia Tian, Yujie Feng, Mingkuo Hai, Yidong Tan, Yan Li, Haoyun Wei

item.title: Goos-H\"anchen Shifts at 458 nm from DUV Dichroic Laser Mirrors
item.description: arXiv:2611.08120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report polarization- and angle-dependent lateral beam shifts observed at 458~nm upon reflection from a deep-ultraviolet (DUV) dichroic multilayer mirror. These Goos--H\"anchen (GH) shifts originate from the phase of the complex Fresnel reflection coefficient and are quantitatively reproduced using a transfer-matrix model. Simultaneous reflectance (R), transmittance (T), and GH shift measurements provide complementary constraints on the coating's amplitude and phase response. The analysis is extended to transmission, predicting analogous phase-induced lateral shifts. In frequency-doubling cavities using dichroic mirrors, these phase effects can accumulate over multiple reflections, leading to deviations from ray-optics predictions that may affect cavity mode structure and resonance conditions. Our results show a GH shift of as much as 2~\textmu m (\bm{$\approx 4.4\lambda$}), which, combined with RT data, enables improved characterization of the phase response of the multilayer coating. The p-polarized reflectance is minimized at a pseudo-Brewster angle of \bm{$\theta_B \approx 46^\circ$} at 458~nm, providing a natural reference point around which the GH shift is enhanced.
item.dc:creator: Shamaila Manzoor, Mauro Chiarotti, Paul J. Robert, Nicola Poli

item.title: An Agent-Driven, Cross-Validated Inverse-Design Pipeline for Dielectric Metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.08127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inverse design of dielectric metasurfaces is powerful but labour-intensive: each new target requires choosing a parameterization and a figure of merit, managing compute resources, and critically assessing results that may be numerically unconverged, sensitive to fabrication errors or trapped in local optima. Here we present an open-source pipeline in which an artificial intelligence (AI) coding agent turns a plain-language specification into metasurface optimization runs, executes them, analyses every run with a fixed checklist and proposes the next iteration. Designs are optimized with differentiable three-dimensional rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA), including robustness to fabrication tolerances, and every reported design is independently verified with finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations. We demonstrate the workflow at 1550 nm on a freeform silicon metagrating, on a polarization-independent meta-atom library assembled into beam-deflecting supercells, and on metalenses built from the same library. In the metagrating case, the independent FDTD verification revealed a 5\% overestimate of the efficiency by the optimization model that a conventional convergence test had not detected, and the robust design retained most of its efficiency under $\pm$10~nm fabrication errors. In the other cases, instead, the obtained RCWA results are confirmed by full-wave simulations.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Emanuele Lio, Roberto Caputo, Alain J. Corso, Maria Guglielmina Pelizzo, Antonio Ferraro

item.title: Analytical Modeling of the Admittance Tensor of Periodic Elliptical Meta-Atoms
item.description: arXiv:2611.08166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A metasurface is an electrically thin interface that controls the phase, amplitude and polarization of a wave, upon reflection or transmission. Printed on a grounded dielectric substrate and spatially modulated across the aperture, it converts a guided surface wave into a radiated leaky wave, a mechanism used in holographic metasurface antennas. Controlling this conversion requires synthesizing a prescribed distribution of admittance tensors, each derived from the homogenization of a subwavelength unit cell. Many numerical and semi-analytical methods have been proposed to relate the geometry of a meta-atom to the tensor it produces. This paper presents, to the author's knowledge, the first analytical model, restricted to elliptical meta-atoms on a uniform lattice. The Galerkin method is applied directly to the geometry of the patches, without spatial meshing. An affine transformation maps any rotated ellipse onto the unit disk, so that a single formulation covers every configuration. A wideband response takes from minutes to tens of minutes with a periodic full-wave solver, while the proposed model evaluates it in a few tens of milliseconds on the same workstation, roughly three orders of magnitude faster. The predicted admittance agrees with a method-of-moments reference up to the fundamental resonance and captures the guided-mode anomaly of the substrate. Beyond the physical insight it brings, the model is a differentiable function of the geometry, which makes the quasi-real-time design of optimized metasurfaces possible.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Froment\`eze

item.title: Machine learning classification of dynamical phases in a driven nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice
item.description: arXiv:2611.08287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driven nonlinear photonic lattices can settle into steady, symmetry-broken, periodic, or chaotic states, and mapping where each occurs in parameter space is key to device design. Brute-force mapping is slow and relies on hand-built criteria, while machine-learning classifiers are usually tested on different systems, so it is unclear which suits a new lattice. We therefore apply four classifiers to the same coherently driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain of Kerr resonators: a hand-built heuristic classifier based on Lyapunov exponents and spectral diagnostics, a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on the heuristic labels, an unsupervised library-building scheme based on augmented dynamic mode decomposition (aDMD), and an unsupervised Gaussian mixture model (GMM) on four dynamical invariants that include an aDMD reconstruction error. Using a converged heuristic diagram as the reference, the CNN reaches 98.0% held-out accuracy, while the two label-free methods reach adjusted Rand indices (ARIs) of 0.916 and 0.947, respectively, without seeing any labels. We show that the aDMD library cleanly resolves the stable and bistable phases and separates symmetric from symmetry-broken periodic oscillations, which the heuristic misses, though it cannot distinguish periodic from chaotic switching. We also find that a poorly converged reference understates the label-free methods' accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Chukwunaedum Patrick Izediuno, Ghada H. Alharbi, Stephan Wong, Zeeshan Ahmad, Sunae So, Minkyung Kim, Sang Soon Oh

item.title: Reprogrammable polaritonic skyrmion and meron lattices based on the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2611.08328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical topological quasiparticles such as skyrmions and merons consist of engineered electromagnetic fields which can be realized via the controlled interference of polaritons. The resulting polaritonic topological lattices offer a promising platform for on-chip information encoding and nanoscale light-matter interaction. However, realizing these functionalities requires active tailoring of the polaritonic topological lattice. Although previous works have achieved tuning of the size of the polaritonic lattice sites, these methods relied on cumbersome and time-consuming fabrication processes and do not allow reconfiguration of the topological invariant. Here, we demonstrate fast optical prototyping of reconfigurable hexagonal and square coupling structures for the generation of polaritonic topological lattices with hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN using the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$. As In$_3$SbTe$_2$ can be switched reversibly between its dielectric ($\varepsilon$>0) amorphous and metallic ($\varepsilon$<0) crystalline phase by laser pulses, metallic In$_3$SbTe$_2$ coupling structures can be optically programmed and reconfigured. Our approach enables tailoring the size of the topological lattice sites by tuning the incident frequency. Moreover, In$_3$SbTe$_2$ allows for tailoring the topological invariant by reprogramming the coupling structure. Our platform enables reprogramming of robust optical topologies within minutes, opening a route toward rewritable on-chip photonic computing based on robust and on demand reconfigurable topological states.
item.dc:creator: Lina J\"ackering, Arvid Schick, Enrico Ba\`u, Lukas Conrads, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Christoph Stampfer, Matthias Wuttig, Andreas Tittl, Thomas Taubner

item.title: Deep-learning surrogate model for rapid quantum-noise computation in dual-pump fiber-optic phase-sensitive amplifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.08437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fiber-optic parametric amplifiers in a phase-sensitive amplifier (PSA) configuration are well known for their low noise properties. Quantum mechanics dictates that these amplifiers can have a 0 dB noise figure (NF) (ratio of signal-to-noise ratio at the input and output of the amplifier) under certain conditions. However, for a dual-pump configuration, when the system is highly nonlinear, fully quantum calculations of NF become non-trivial. In such cases, semi-quantum models of NF evaluation exists, however, they are often complicated and resource intensive. To simplify that, in this work, first we use a semi-quantum NF calculation framework for the generation of numerically simulated input-output dataset of NF over a large parameter spaces. Then we use the data to train an optimized deep neural network (DNN) for rapid NF prediction. Utilizing the DNN, we demonstrate about 400 times reduction in the computation time compared to the standard semi-quantum NF evaluation approach with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0015 dB. Using clustering we demonstrate a rapid exploration of the parameter space with respect to high gain (20 dB) and low NF (0.3 dB) targets and retrieve associated design parameters. These results illustrate the efficacy of machine learning-based approaches for rapid search of high-dimensional parameter spaces especially in compute intensive photonic systems.
item.dc:creator: Yousra Bouasria, Debanuj Chatterjee, Abdessamad Belfakir, Debabrota Basu

item.title: Topological Transitions of Evanescent Waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.07038v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the band structure of evanescent waves, that is, the decaying or growing solutions that live within the gaps of tight-binding Hamiltonians. Although the underlying Hamiltonian is Hermitian, these modes carry complex wavevectors and therefore exhibit a non-Hermitian dispersion. Using the transfer matrix formalism in one dimension, we show that, in addition to the standard exceptional points that appear at the band edges, a different type of exceptional point can arise inside the gap, protected by spinless time-reversal symmetry. Tuning model parameters drives a topological transition where such in-gap exceptional points are nucleated in pairs, mediated by a crossing between purely imaginary momentum branches. We show that this spectral structure is diagnosed by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index assigned to every energy inside the gap, with the in-gap exceptional points arising as its domain walls. A generic bound state in the system has a tail that is purely exponential when its energy lies between a band edge and the nearest exceptional point, but becomes oscillatory - with a wavevector differing from the band-edge momentum - when its energy lies between the pair of in-gap exceptional points. We illustrate these results using continuum and tight-binding models, as well as an anisotropic photonic crystal.
item.dc:creator: Ignacio Pavez, Tom Sheppard, Yoonseok Hwang, Hannah M. Price, Frank Schindler

item.title: Dark-State Coherent Control of Excitons in TMD Monolayers: A Reduced Intravalley Lindblad Framework for WSe$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2611.07315v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dark-state coherence in driven three-level systems underlies electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) and stimulated Raman adiabatic passage (STIRAP). Their performance depends on the coupling topology: in a ladder ($\Xi$) scheme the coherence can bypass a lossy intermediate state, whereas in a $V$ scheme it is carried by two excited states that both decay. We develop a topology-resolved Lindblad framework for driven three-level excitonic manifolds at fixed center-of-mass momentum, in which a single exciton couples to phonons, the radiation field and a dilute exciton gas. The $\Xi$ and $V$ manifolds are selected from the exciton spectrum by systematically screening optical brightness, intra-excitonic dipole strength and state compactness, making the selection reproducible and transferable to other materials. Within this framework, in the $\Xi$ manifold of hBN-encapsulated WSe$_2$, a weak optical pulse, preceded by a terahertz pulse in the counterintuitive STIRAP order, converts the excitation it creates into an optically dark exciton by dark-state following, while the lossy bright intermediate exciton stays nearly empty. The conversion is limited by emission from that intermediate state rather than by non-adiabatic coupling, and is controlled by a single adiabaticity parameter of the terahertz leg. The exchange mean field of the exciton gas shifts the two-photon resonance by more than the conversion tolerates at moderate densities; the center of the cascade transparency window provides an in situ calibration, and we identify the control strengths at which it is true EIT rather than Autler--Townes splitting. The $V$ manifold loses its coherence on the radiative timescale and serves as the unprotected reference. These results provide a minimal, material-specific baseline for dark-state coherent control of excitons in two-dimensional semiconductors in the radiative limit.
item.dc:creator: Mauricio Martinez, Martin A. Mosquera

item.title: Ultrafast Moir\'e Exciton Dynamics Revealed by Two-Dimensional Coherent Spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.07539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Moir\'e superlattices of van der Waals heterostructures confine excitons into discrete energy levels in finite-sized samples, yet their internal relaxation pathways remain obscured by inhomogeneous broadening. Here, using two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS), we directly resolve seven discrete energy levels of the moir\'e-confined intralayer $\mathrm{WS}_{2}$ A exciton in an hBN-encapsulated $\mathrm{WS}_{2}/\mathrm{WSe}_{2}$ heterostructure, corresponding to a confinement depth of 57.02 meV. By tracking the population of these levels over picosecond delays, we uncover a two-stage thermalization process: an effective exciton temperature drops from 171.8 to 99.3 K within 1.2 ps through rapid intra-manifold population redistribution, followed by a slower recovery toward quasi-equilibrium mediated by exciton--environment interactions. Kullback--Leibler divergence analysis confirms the progressive transition from a non-equilibrium to a Boltzmann-distributed population. Our results establish state-resolved access to moir\'e exciton dynamics and provide a foundation for exploring nonequilibrium many-body phenomena in moir\'e quantum materials.
item.dc:creator: Deran Zhang, Zhexue Chen, Dongxue Chen, Tengfei Yan, Jianhua Jiang, Hui Dong

item.title: Multi-Channel Non-Abelian Edge Pumping via Multi-Degeneracy Encircling
item.description: arXiv:2611.07594v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Non-Abelian operations enable sequence-dependent control of light, yet experimental realizations in wave systems have remained confined to local bulk or same-boundary modes and have often required fragile gap-closing degeneracies. Conventional Thouless pumps, meanwhile, support only two-channel edge transfer across a single gap. Here we demonstrate multi-channel non-Abelian edge pumping on a silicon photonic chip by adiabatically encircling multiple band degeneracies in a multi-gap lattice. In a minimal three-band band-triangle, two opposite-charge Weyl points and one zero-charge degeneracy are linked by global band connectivity, yielding both opposite-boundary and same-boundary edge channels. Sequencing these channels produces non-Abelian braiding of three topologically protected edge modes that reside on distinct physical boundaries. The process remains fully gapped and is protected by topological winding rather than by maintained spectral degeneracies. The same band-triangle principle extends systematically to an arbitrary number of channels, establishing a scalable route to collective, sequence-controlled routing of topological states in integrated photonic circuits.
item.dc:creator: Qingyang Mo, Jiacheng Sun, Zhongfu Li, Jiajun Li, Wange Song, Tao Li, Shuang Zhang

item.title: Bringing Dark States to Light after Frustrated Tunneling Ionization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07764v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in gases is typically regarded as a sub-laser-cycle process, well described by the semiclassical three-step model. In this work, we report the extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) emission observed in an HHG experiment arising from a longer temporal process associated with dark states populated through frustrated tunneling ionization. The emission exhibits a larger spatial divergence than typical high-order harmonics, resembling the polarization decay of optically bright states. Supported by the time-frequency analysis of the theoretical calculations, we show that the emission originates from the nonradiative capture of the tunneling electrons into excited dark states of the neutral atom, followed by Floquet-like laser-dressing effects induced by the extended tail of the driving pulse. Our results reveal a largely unexplored pathway for XUV generation through laser-dressed dark states, thereby enabling the enhancement of coherent XUV emission at targeted wavelengths with high repetition rates.
item.dc:creator: Yu He, Eleni Tzima, Gergana D. Borisova, Noah L. Wach, Aaron T. Bondy, Juan C. Del Valle, Klaus Bartschat, Christian Ott, Thomas Pfeifer

item.title: Spectrotemporal imaging of ultrafast electron dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.07884v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We demonstrate a spectrotemporal imaging technique that maps ultrafast electron dynamics onto energy- and angle-resolved photoelectron distributions in a single measurement. The underlying principle is to encode the probing time into the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons, while the evolving quantum dynamics is retrieved from their angular distributions. We experimentally demonstrate this concept by imaging spin-orbit wave packet dynamics in resonance-enhanced multiphoton ionization of potassium atoms using two complementary approaches. In the first, three spectrally distinct probe pulses sample the dynamics at selected delays and map the corresponding wave packet configurations onto separate photoelectron energy channels. In the second, a single broadband chirped probe pulse establishes a continuous time-to-energy mapping through its time-dependent instantaneous frequency, thereby encoding the evolution of the wave packet across a broad photoelectron energy band. The resulting photoelectron momentum distribution exhibits a characteristic fork-shaped pattern. Combining supercontinuum pulse shaping with velocity map imaging, we experimentally resolve the spin-orbit dynamics over a time window exceeding 300 fs, in good agreement with quantum dynamical simulations. Our results establish spectrotemporal photoelectron imaging as a versatile approach to time-resolved spectroscopy, replacing sequential delay scans by parallel acquisition of ultrafast quantum dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Darius K\"ohnke, Kai Ebken, Tim Bayer, Matthias Wollenhaupt

item.title: Phase-Matched Design of Pinching-Antenna Elements on a 60-GHz Dielectric Rod Waveguide
item.description: arXiv:2611.07954v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The radiation of pinching antennas, dielectric elements placed on a dielectric waveguide, depends on the element shape. We explain it with a phase-matching, or prism-coupler, picture: the guided rod mode couples into the denser antenna plate at an angle set by the plate-mode effective index, about 31 degrees at 60 GHz, and radiates through the face it reaches first. This yields a simple sizing rule linking element height to contact length. Rectangular, isosceles and right-triangular elements of equal contact length and height are compared from 53 to 67 GHz in full-wave openEMS simulations including the waveguide-to-rod transitions. The rectangle peaks sharply at the rule, reaching 15.9 dBi. The right triangle keeps its gain within 0.7 dB and its side lobes at least 10 dB down over a two-to-one height range. At the rule, both outperform the isosceles element by 1.2 to 2.1 dB, and all remain matched.
item.dc:creator: Stylianos D. Asimonis, Dimitrios Tyrovolas, Spyridon Daskalakis, Nikos C. Sagias, Donal P. Lynch, George K. Karagiannidis

item.title: Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
item.description: arXiv:2611.08444v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.
item.dc:creator: Armando Angrisani, Hela Mhiri

item.title: Dynamical effects induced by synthetic SU(1,1) gauge fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.08447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter. Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field. The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.
item.dc:creator: Chenwei Lv

item.title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.
item.dc:creator: Ke-Sean J. M. Peter, Ryan A. Kowalski, David A. Curie, Dakota Braaten, Matthew W. Day, Denis R. Candido, Deyu Li, Richard F. Haglund, Joshua D. Caldwell, Richarda Niemann

item.title: Nonperturbative regime of low-order harmonic generation in intense low-frequency laser field
item.description: arXiv:2512.06816v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We find the atomic response to the intense femtosecond laser pulse via solving numerically the three-dimensional non-stationary Schr\"odinger equation (TDSE) for a model atom and calculating its dipole moment. For weak quasi-static fields, the response is well described by a perturbation approach, but for intensities higher than about $0.6 \, \, 10^{14}$ W/cm$^2$ the accuracy of this description is unsatisfactory, regardless of the order of non-linearity taken into account. We suggest fitting the numerical TDSE solution results with a Pad\'e expansion, and show that this approximation describes the response well both in the perturbative regime and beyond it for intensities approximately up to $1.4 \, \, 10^{14}$ W/cm$^2$. To consider the non-perturbative nonlinearity beyond the quasi-static limit we use the model of nonlinear oscillator with the restoring force defined by the found Pad\'e expression. Our model fails to predict the behaviour of the nonlinear refractive index in the nonperturbative domain, but it describes well the nonperturbative growth of the efficiency with the laser intensity for other nonlinear optical processes, namely, the third and fifth harmonic generation in the IR field and the optical rectification in a two-color field.
item.dc:creator: S. A. Bondarenko, V. V. Strelkov

item.title: Digitally enhanced Multi-wavelength Stabilization using a Passive Fiber Frequency Reference
item.description: arXiv:2610.01575v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-stability frequency stabilization between lasers is essential for applications such as precision metrology, frequency dissemination, and quantum communications. We demonstrate the use of code-based multiplexing of a passive fiber-based interferometer for frequency stabilization and transfer between lasers separated by 85 GHz in frequency using a single shared passive reference. Out-of-loop characterization places an upper bound of sub-kHz/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ on the transferred frequency noise at Fourier frequencies above 40 mHz, with a differential fractional stability of $7\times10^{-13}$ at 1 second. We also demonstrate continuous laser tunability and characterize the residual length noise coupling. Finally, we provide a framework for scaling the architecture to higher laser counts, offering a pathway to scalable, frequency agile stabilization of multiple light sources without the overhead of an optical frequency comb.
item.dc:creator: Hilma Karlsson, Vaishali Adya, Robert L. Ward, Chathura P. Bandutunga

item.title: Nonperturbative optomechanics with thin, weakly reflective intracavity dielectrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.15749v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Levitated dielectric sensors are often treated as perturbative probes of a pre-existing optical field. We show that this picture fails for a novel sensor geometry: a dielectric plate whose transverse extent captures the full optical mode. Even an optically thin sensor with modest refractive index can heavily restructure the intracavity fields, effectively partitioning a cavity into two subcavities with substantial cross-coupling and producing new optical resonances and trapping sites with properties which deviate from the standard intuition. Conventional perturbative expressions for the cavity frequency shift and optomechanical coupling depart from the exact solution at thicknesses as small as $\sim\lambda/(10n)$. Furthermore, cavity locking decreases the coupling and increases the trap stiffness by orders of magnitude, and the coupled subcavity structure permits appreciable optical cooling at zero detuning, a distinct behavior unique to this nonperturbative regime. These effects, sharing a common origin, establish a distinct regime of cavity optomechanics in which the sensor is no longer merely a probe of the cavity field, but an element that helps define it.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Laeuger, Nancy Aggarwal

item.title: Optical Coherent Combining in Multi-Aperture Free-Space Receivers through Atmospheric Turbulence via Optically Computed Alignment Gradients
item.description: arXiv:2610.21876v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-aperture reception yields a coherent-combining gain only if the aperture fields are aligned in phase and polarization, which in a downlink must track the atmosphere. We show that the exact gradients of the combined power with respect to the phase and polarization angle of each branch can be measured optically, before photodetection: a passive tap of the combined field, split one-to-$N$, is the common self-reference and, interfered with a branch tap on a 3 dB coupler, yields the phase gradient; with a $90^\circ$ Faraday rotator and a static $\pi/2$ offset it yields the polarization gradient. Each branch then runs fixed-gain phase and polarization loops, without division, perturbation, dither, reference laser, or per-branch receiver, as analog integrators or a low-rate processor. We derive the gradients, their optical readout, and the loop stability condition. A phase-only simulation with identical disturbances, a common 100 MS/s clock, and retuning of every scheme compares the loop with centralized and distributed stochastic parallel gradient descent and with dither locking at the OSNR where ideal four-beam combining reaches the 28 GBd DP-QPSK FEC threshold. Up to $10^5$ rad/s of multi-tone disturbance the loop keeps the lowest residual loss, at most $5.6\times10^{-4}$ dB for four beams and 13 to 160 times below the alternatives, and reaches $90\%$ efficiency in 0.6 $\mu$s for up to 64 beams. The taps leave the receiver OSNR unchanged and every retuned scheme stays within 0.06 dB of ideal combining, whereas brief dither misalignments cost 0.14 dB. Up to $10^7$ rad/s it preserves the ideal-combining bit-error ratio for four, sixteen, and sixty-four beams while every baseline crosses the threshold and slips carrier recovery. In fades it loses $4\times10^{-3}$ dB where the others lose 0.2 to 0.9 dB. Assumptions and limitations are stated; experimental validation remains open.
item.dc:creator: Chen Cheng (Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China), Tong Luo (Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China), Siyu Gong (Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China), Qun Zhang (Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China), Linsheng Fan (Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China), Qi Wu (Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China), Yanfu Yang (Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, China), Jiayin Xue (Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China)

item.title: Contrast-Enhanced Nonlinear Imaging with Moir\'e Flatband Superlattices
item.description: arXiv:2611.03951v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nonlinear metasurfaces offer a compact platform for infrared-to-visible conversion and imaging, yet resonant enhancement is often accompanied by restricted angular acceptance, limiting the range of transverse spatial frequencies that can interact efficiently with the nonlinear modes. Here, we address this challenge using a one-dimensional photonic moir\'e superlattice supporting multiple quasi-flat bands in the near-infrared. These moir\'e modes combine strong near-field enhancement with broad momentum-space accessibility, enabling efficient third-harmonic generation (THG) while maintaining stable excitation over a large angular range. Experimentally, we observe strong THG emission near $467~\mathrm{nm}$ under broadband excitation from $ 1180$ to $ 2000~\mathrm {nm} $. We further employ the nonlinear moir\'e superlattice for infrared imaging by converting an infrared target into visible through the THG process. By encoding image information into displacement-dependent THG signals and decoding their spatial variations, we experimentally resolve weak features and internal textures with improved contrast compared with THG imaging using nonlinear films or conventional nonlinear metasurfaces. These results establish photonic moir\'e superlattices as a versatile platform combining efficient frequency conversion, broad angular acceptance, and mode-sensitive spatial encoding for high-contrast, label-free nonlinear imaging with enhanced feature discrimination.
item.dc:creator: Amin Zamani, Lihang Feng, Jianji Liu, Ze Zheng, Gabriel Sanderson, Mohsen Rahmani, Peilong Hong, Lei Xu

item.title: Optimizing the statistical power of negative-partial-transpose-based entanglement tests
item.description: arXiv:2502.19624v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A key requirement of any separable quantum state is that its density matrix has a non-negative partial transpose. For continuous bipartite quantum states, violation of this condition may be tested via the hierarchy of negative-partial-transpose (NPT) based entanglement criteria introduced by Shchukin and Vogel [Phys. Rev. Lett. 95, 230502 (2005)]. However, even for a known state, a procedure to determine the optimal NPT-based criterion within the hierarchy has, thus far, remained outstanding. Here, we introduce a theoretical framework and numerical toolbox NPyT to compare criteria performance via the statistical power of hypothesis testing for a known input state to enable the optimal entanglement criterion to be determined. Our framework takes into account environmental noise and finite number of measurements, and optimally allocates measurement resources. To demonstrate the utility of our approach, we apply our statistical framework to prominent examples of Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, including the two-mode squeezed vacuum state, the quanta-subtracted two-mode squeezed vacuum state, and the two-mode Schr\"odinger-cat state. We discuss the optimal criteria identified for these states and compare them to other commonly employed criteria. For example, we identify an entanglement test for the two-mode squeezed vacuum state that has high statistical power and outperforms Simon's criterion. This work illustrates that the non-Gaussianity of the entanglement test distribution increases with test matrix size, and highlights that smaller test matrices generally provide better performance. Beyond bipartite inseparability, our framework can be extended to a wide variety of other matrix-based tests of nonclassicality and multi-mode entanglement.
item.dc:creator: Lydia A. Kanari-Naish, Amaya Calvo-S\'anchez, Jack Clarke, Arjun Gupta, Sofia Qvarfort, Michael R. Vanner

item.title: Statistical properties of quantum jumps between macroscopic states of light: reading an operational coherence record
item.description: arXiv:2512.07754v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose an experimental apparatus to reveal the quantum coherence manifested in downward quantum jumps of amplitude bistability. The underlying coherent superposition of macroscopic quantum states is translated into the statistical properties of the integrated charge deposited in the detector circuit of a mode-matched heterodyne/homodyne detection scheme. At first, the dynamical evolution of a signal transmitted from an auxiliary cavity is employed to pinpoint a macroscopic switching event in a bistable main cavity subject to direct photodetection. Once the decision is made on the occurrence of a downward switch, the main cavity mode is let to freely decay to the vacuum, monitored to the production of an integrated charge. In the long-time limit, the charge distribution over an identical collection of pure states generated during the jumps converges to the Q function (heterodyne detection) or marginals of the Wigner function (homodyne detection) dictated by the phase of the local oscillator. When fluctuations over the ensemble step in, we connect the statistical properties of several switching events and the ensuing production of current records, to the cavity field correlations associated with the breakdown of photon blockade.
item.dc:creator: Th. K. Mavrogordatos

item.title: Reflective Metastructure Q-plate for Ultrashort Laser Pulses
item.description: arXiv:2606.12041v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The orbital angular momentum of light is an intriguing property for developing light driven applications. It emerged as an independent degree of freedom by which to manipulate light and, consequently, the interaction of light with matter. Several methods exist for the generation of light carrying orbital angular momentum, mostly employing transmitting or reflecting optical components, which radially modulate the phase profile of the light. As one of such components, transmissive q-plates established themselves as standard elements due to their usability over a broad wavelength range. Here, we present our approach to building a highly reflective q-plate with a diameter of 4.5 mm based on a plasmonic metasurface capable of converting orbital angular momentum from the nanostructure to ultrashort laser pulses without measurable temporal broadening under the investigated conditions. We highlight its working principle over a wide range of wavelengths for reflection under normal and grazing incidence.
item.dc:creator: Christopher G. O. Wei{\ss}, Ellen Brennfleck, Bert L\"agel, Laurenz Rettig, Benjamin Stadtm\"uller, Martin Aeschlimann, Tobias Eul

item.title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.01993v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, each class's Born probability above its no-information share, $P_g - b_g$, splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM). The split itself follows from known results on quadratic forms: with the transmitted light held fixed, it is what Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline and the Shapley value give. What we add is a way to measure it on the hardware that classifies, from class probabilities on a quantum chip or, in simulation, from camera frames on a lens bench, with no gradient circuit and no light sent backwards; a $g\times g$ map takes $1 + 2g^2$ runs. Deleting the 5% of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73% to 9% (one seed), as occlusion and gradient $\times$ input do, while plain gradients remove much less. The classifiers share one architecture, a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a fixed Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at one wavelength reach 72.3% on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask computed classically before approximate loading, 300 test pictures were classified at 37.7% against 10% chance (56.3% in exact simulation), and $2\times2$ maps of the filtered input of 30 test pictures drawn at random in advance, measured on the chip, agreed with the exact ones ($r = 0.88$; standard estimator 0.82). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data; as the trim that removed it was chosen on test pictures, the Caltech-10 results are exploratory.
item.dc:creator: Teerawat Tongloy, Rangsan Jomtarak
